texts.exact_text: In Phî there is the want of good understanding between the (different classes of) men, and its indication is unfavourable to the firm and correct course of the superior man. We see in it the great gone and the little come.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 12; scan-backed transcription p. 83, hexagram statement
texts.notes: Legge's title restored from the source statement.

texts.exact_text: The first SIX, divided, suggests the idea of grass pulled up, and bringing with it other stalks with whose roots it is connected. With firm correctness (on the part of its subject), there will be good fortune and progress.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 12; scan-backed transcription p. 83, line 1

texts.exact_text: The second SIX, divided, shows its subject patient and obedient. To the small man (comporting himself so) there will be good fortune. If the great man (comport himself) as the distress and obstruction require, he will have success.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 12; scan-backed transcription p. 83, line 2

texts.exact_text: The third SIX, divided, shows its subject ashamed of the purpose folded (in his breast).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 12; scan-backed transcription p. 83, line 3

texts.exact_text: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows its subject acting in accordance with the ordination (of Heaven), and committing no error. His companions will come and share in his happiness.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 12; scan-backed transcription p. 83, line 4

texts.exact_text: In the fifth NINE, undivided, we see him who brings the distress and obstruction to a close, -- the great man and fortunate. (But let him say), 'We may perish! We may perish!' (so shall the state of things become firm, as if) bound to a clump of bushy mulberry trees.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 12; scan-backed transcription p. 83, line 5

texts.exact_text: The sixth NINE, undivided, shows the overthrow (and removal of) the condition of distress and obstruction. Before this there was that condition. Hereafter there will be joy.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 12; scan-backed transcription p. 83, line 6

texts.exact_text:
The form of Phî, it will be seen, is exactly the opposite of that of Thâi. Much of what has been said on the interpretation of that will apply to this, or at least assist the student in making out the meaning of its symbolism. Phî is the hexagram of the seventh month. Genial influences have done their work, the processes of growth are at an end. Henceforth increasing decay must be looked for.

Naturally we should expect the advance of the subject of the first of the three weak lines to lead to evil; but if he set himself to be firm and correct, he will bring about a different issue.

Patience and obedience are proper for the small man in all circumstances. If the great man in difficulty yet cherish these attributes, he will soon have a happy issue out of the distress.

The third line is weak. Its place is odd, and therefore for it incorrect. Its subject would vent his evil purpose, but has not strength to do so. He is left therefore to the shame which he ought to feel without a word of warning. Does the ming of the fourth line mean the ordination of Heaven, as Zhū Xī thinks; or the orders of the ruler, as Guǎn Zǐ) says? Whichever interpretation be taken (and some critics unite the two), the action of the subject of the line, whose strength is tempered by the even position, will be good and correct, and issue in success and happiness.

The strong line in the fifth, (its correct), place, brings the distress and obstruction to a close. Yet its subject -- the ruler in the hexagram - is warned to continue to be cautious in two lines of rhyme: --

'And let him say, "I die! I die I" So to a bushy clump his fortune he shall tie.'

There is an end of the condition of distress. It was necessary, that condition should give place to its opposite; and the strong line in the topmost place fitly represents the consequent joy. 否 ䷋
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 12; scan-backed transcription p. 83, notes

texts.exact_text: 否之匪人，不利君子貞，大往小來。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 易經卦辭

texts.exact_text: 否之匪人，不利君子貞，大往小來。則是天地不交而萬物不通也，上下不交而天下无邦也。內陰而外陽，內柔而外剛，內小人而外君子，小人道長，君子道消也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 彖

texts.exact_text: 天地不交，否；君子以儉德辟難，不可榮以祿。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 大象

texts.exact_text: 初六，拔茅茹以其彙，貞吉。亨。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 爻 1

texts.exact_text: 拔茅貞吉，志在君也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 小象 1

texts.exact_text: 六二，包承，小人吉，大人否。亨。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 爻 2

texts.exact_text: 大人否，亨。不亂羣也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 小象 2

texts.exact_text: 六三，包羞。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 爻 3

texts.exact_text: 包羞，位不當也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 小象 3

texts.exact_text: 九四，有命，无咎，疇離祉。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 爻 4

texts.exact_text: 有命无咎，志行也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 小象 4

texts.exact_text: 九五，休否，大人吉。其亡其亡，繫于苞桑。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 爻 5

texts.exact_text: 大人之吉，位正當也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 小象 5

texts.exact_text: 上九，傾否，先否後喜。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 爻 6

texts.exact_text: 否終則傾，何可長也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/否; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 12, 小象 6

texts.exact_text: 'The want of good understanding between the (different classes of) men in Phî, and its indication as unfavourable to the firm and correct course of the superior man; with the intimation that the great are gone and the little come:' -- all this springs from the fact that in it heaven and earth are not in communication with each other, and all things in consequence do not have free course; and that the high and the low (superiors and inferiors) are not in communication with one another, and there are no (well-regulated) states under the sky. The inner (trigram ☷) is made up of the weak and divided lines, and the outer of the strong and undivided (trigram ☰): the inner is (the symbol of) weakness, and the outer of strength; the inner (represents) the small man, and the outer the superior man. Thus the way of the small man appears increasing, and that of the superior man decreasing.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix I, Hexagram 12, p. 225

texts.exact_text: (The trigrams ☰ ☷ of) heaven and earth, not in intercommunication, form Phî. The superior man, in accordance with this, restrains (the manifestation) of) his virtue, and avoids the calamities (that threaten him). There is no opportunity of conferring on him the glory of emolument.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 12, p. 283

texts.exact_text: 'The good fortune through firm goodness, (suggested by) the pulling up of the grass,' arises from the will (of the parties intended) being bent on (serving) the ruler.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 12, line 1, p. 283

texts.exact_text: 'The great man, comporting himself as the distress and obstruction require, will have success:' -- he does not allow himself to be disordered by the herd (of small men).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 12, line 2, p. 283

texts.exact_text: That 'his shame is folded in his breast' is owing to the inappropriateness of his position.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 12, line 3, p. 283

texts.exact_text: 'He acts in accordance with the ordination (of Heaven), and commits no error:' -- the purpose of his mind can be carried into effect.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 12, line 4, p. 283

texts.exact_text: 'The good fortune of the great man' arises from the correctness of his position.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 12, line 5, p. 283

texts.exact_text: 'The distress and obstruction having reached its end, it is overthrown and removed:' -- how could it be prolonged?
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 12, line 6, p. 283
